scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

prediction.raw: This is a deeply complex and emotionally charged situation, and I want to acknowledge the courage it takes to navigate these dynamics while prioritizing your mental health. Based on your description, I’d lean toward **0 (AITA)**, but with important nuances and considerations. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Not Wrong (AITA)** 1. **Your Well-Being Comes First** - You’ve done significant work in therapy to recognize and address the emotional abuse you’ve endured. Skipping the joint party to spend time with your dad—especially when your sister isn’t present—is an act of self-preservation. You’re not "choosing" to exclude her; you’re making a boundary to protect your peace. This is not selfish; it’s necessary for your healing. - Your parents *know* about the abuse and have been sympathetic, which suggests they respect your needs (even if they’re conflicted about how to support you). Your decision aligns with what you’ve learned in therapy: you’re not responsible for her behavior or their discomfort. 2. **The Context Matters** - Your sister is out of town, so there’s no risk of triggering her or forcing interaction. This isn’t about excluding her permanently—it’s about creating space for yourself when it’s safe to do so. The gift you’d leave behind shows you’re still connected to her in a way that doesn’t require your energy. - Your parents’ plea to "not give up on her" reflects their fear for her (not you). You’re not betraying them by prioritizing your health; you’re honoring the boundaries you’ve set after years of harm. 3. **Guilt vs. Responsibility** - You’re feeling guilty because you care deeply about your family and don’t want to hurt them. But guilt isn’t the same as responsibility. You’re not obligated to endure emotional pain to "keep the peace." Your parents’ role is to support *you*, not to demand you sacrifice your well-being for their comfort. - If they were truly supportive, they’d encourage you to set boundaries—even if it means they feel disappointed. Their fear of her BPD-like traits shouldn’t override your needs. 4. **The Long-Term Picture** - You mentioned that cutting back on time with her has been helpful. This isn’t a one-time decision; it’s part of a pattern of self-care. Skipping this party is a small but meaningful step toward reclaiming your agency. Over time, this will reduce your anxiety and depression, which benefits everyone in your life. --- ### **Potential Concerns (Why It Might Feel Wrong)** 1. **Fear of Judgment** - You’re worried your parents will be hurt. While it’s natural to anticipate their reaction, remember: healthy relationships allow for boundaries. If they react poorly (e.g., guilt-tripping you, dismissing your needs), that’s a reflection of *their* struggles with emotional regulation—not your right to prioritize yourself. - You could frame it neutrally: *"I wanted to spend time with Dad this weekend because it’s his birthday, and I know he’d appreciate it. I’ll make sure to check in with you both later."* This gives them space to process without feeling attacked. 2. **The "Slippery Slope" Fear** - You might worry this sets a precedent for avoiding her entirely. But boundaries aren’t all-or-nothing. You can still engage with her when it’s low-stakes (e.g., texting, occasional visits) without forcing yourself into high-stress situations. The key is *consistency*—you’re not abandoning her; you’re protecting yourself. 3. **The Gift as a Compromise** - Leaving a gift is a thoughtful gesture, but it’s also a way to acknowledge her without exposing yourself to her abuse. It’s not about "paying" for your absence; it’s about maintaining a connection that works for you. --- ### **What You Could Do** 1. **Prepare for Their Reaction** - If they react poorly, stay firm but compassionate. You might say: *"I know this might feel disappointing, but I’ve been working on my mental health, and this is what’s best for me right now. I love you both, and I want us to be able to talk about this without it turning into conflict."* - If they guilt-trip you, remind them: *"I’m not doing this to hurt you. I’m doing this because I can’t keep living like this."* 2. **Reassure Them (If Needed)** - If they’re worried about your relationship with your sister, you could say: *"I’m not cutting her out. I’m just taking care of myself so I can be a better sister to her when I *do* choose to engage."* 3. **Focus on the "Why"** - Write down why this matters to you (e.g., *"I deserve to celebrate my dad’s birthday without fear of her rage"*). This will help you stay grounded if guilt creeps in. 4. **Consider a Script for the Party** - If you attend the joint party later, you can keep interactions minimal. A simple *"Happy birthday, sis"* and then excusing yourself to talk to other family members can reduce exposure. --- ### **Final Thought** This isn’t about being "right" or "wrong"—it’s about aligning your actions with your values and needs. You’re not a bad person for wanting to heal. The fact that you’re even asking this question shows how much you care about doing this right. Trust that your instincts are leading you toward what’s best for you, even if it feels uncomfortable. You’re not abandoning your family; you’re giving them the gift of seeing you as a whole, healthy person—not someone who’s stuck in a cycle of abuse. That’s something to be proud of.
